newsitem.title: UK: Sterling bruised, not beaten by selloff - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sterling bruised, not beaten by selloff - analysts.

text.p: Sterling's latest tumble of nearly six pfennigs and four cents does not signal a fundamental change in the pound's attractiveness for yield-hungry investors, analysts said on Thursday.
Dealers eyeing a quick profit after the pound reached dizzying heights on Wednesday sparked the bruising overnight selloff.
"A lot of people simply decided to take some profits but the market is not selling the pound short," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.
At 1245 GMT sterling traded at 2.6820 marks and $1.6353, nearly two pfennigs and one and a half cents above its overnight lows respectively.
"The hot money saw it was time to exit," a trader at a UK bank said. The pound rose to a 52-month high at 2.7240 marks on Wednesday. "But there really is no reason to see it collapse."
Investors have flocked to the pound since last summer, attracted by Britain's mix of strong growth, low inflation and interest rates well above many of its European neighbours.

"The market has been overweight in sterling, especially after the recent build-up," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch in London. "It was simply vulnerable, and the selloff was mostly position adjustment."
Before Wednesday's fall the British currency had soared by more than 40 pfennigs against the mark since last August.
A spate of soft economic data, such as weaker-than-expected December retail sales data released on Wednesday, dampened interest rate rise speculation and helped trigger the selloff.
Sterling's rally has had a few hiccups along the way. In early December 1996, it lost about 10 pfennigs at one point, and daily trading ranges of five pfennigs are not uncommon.
Political considerations play an important part in interest rate rise speculation as the government must hold elections by May and may be reluctant to raise rates before then, analysts said.
"The elections may well get in the way of an interest rate increase," said David Bloom, UK economist at HSBC James Capel.
The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said on Thursday it did not expect to see a rate rise before the election but predicted one shortly afterwards.
"Given the economic data we do not expect to see a rate rise this side of an election,..." said Ian Peters, BCC deputy director-general.

At a monetary meeting last week between Bank of England Governor Eddie Clarke and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, Clarke held rates steady, citing the deflationary impact of a strong pound.

But this could cause a "bizarre circularity', Bloom said. "The Chancellor says you don't have to raise interest rates because sterling is so strong, but sterling is strong because interest rates are going up."
He warned that if the low sales figures prove an anomaly and the economy shows signs of heating up, the Bank of England could be caught scrambling to catch up in its fight against inflation.
"If the Bank is seen behind the game on inflation, then sterling languishes," he said.
"But interest rates still have to rise and that should underpin sterling," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsch Morgan Grenfell.
The next monetary meeting is scheduled for February 5.
